```

- WHY. PR-357 read the land/leave pair and left one honest open item
  about the port: "whether the port's ask model needs the delta". It
  does, and that is not something a record can assert from the dis alone
  once the model exists - it has to be run. So this PR is the small
  port half of that read: the two methods in `ll_seq.c` where the
  element's other position arithmetic already lives (`ll_seq_anchor_origin`
  reads f0/f2 with the same sentinel test), and one leg that proves the
  arithmetic AND its effect on the standing query that PR-352 modelled in
  the same file.

- WHAT IS MODELLED. `ll_seq_anchor_land(e, facing, &x, &y)` and
  `ll_seq_anchor_leave` in `ported/ll_seq.c`, with the instruction
  citations in their comments: the `movsx`/`cmp 0x7fff`/`je` guard that
  writes nothing, the y leg `f2 - f6`, the x leg `f0 - f4` taken the
  other way for a non-positive facing (0x429a0's `test ebx,ebx`/`jle`),
  and the leave method as the exact inverse (0x429ec, 0x429fb, 0x42a0d).
  They take a POSITION PAIR exactly as the engine does - `edx` is the
  object itself at 0x238b0 and at the four script runners, or a copy of
  `[obj+0x00]/[obj+0x04]` at 0x53df0's `[obj+0x89]` - and the caller
  supplies the facing, which is `[obj+0x6d]` in the class verbs and the
  +0x50 verb's answer in the other six sites.

- WHAT IS NOT DONE, AND WHY THAT IS THE RIGHT STOP. Nothing calls them
  from the level path. The engine's argument is the CURRENT FRAME'S
  .SEQ element, reached through `[view+0x48]`, and the port does not
  model that per-frame element identity for a level object; more to the
  point, PR-357's measurement of what shipped elements actually carry is
  still open and needs a staged fixture. Wiring an offset nobody has
  measured would put an unproven number into the runtime. What this PR
  does instead is make the law executable and pinned by five mutations,
  so the day the census is run the wiring is a small, testable step.

- THE LEG'S MEASUREMENT IN ONE LINE (printed by `./ll_level
  --mov-selftest`, prefix `land shift:`): a seat table 12 px above the
  requester's row is refused by 0x45400 from his own row; after a
  landing whose element declares that second anchor the same law
  ANSWERS; the mirrored x leg of the same landing takes the ask past the
  table's last record and it is refused again. Landing is a placement
  step, and it moves the point every surface query is asked from.

- LEDGER NOTE. `tools/jq.py oi OI-128` (the user's PR-358 fix) now lists
  all 7 records that name OI-128 with prose/structured marked apart, and
  a bare `0x33` routes to the free-text search instead of an empty addr
  query - both used in this pass, both working as the record describes.

MEASURED: (a) THE POPULATION. /tmp/opencode/pr360_anchor_census.py walks
  the containers with verify_seq.records_of (the walk make verify-seq
  pins) and parses every payload with tools/seq_parse.py: 1655 payloads
  plus the one known-bad original (ANIMACJE/TUNGA.11/DNGANI/OGIEN_M.SEQ,
  accepted as at PR-47), 14715 elements, every one consumed exactly.
  185 elements (1.26%) hold 0x7fff in f0 - the guard case, where
  0x4298d writes nothing - and they are spread one per file over 182
  payloads: 169 of them are ANIBACK background strips (mostly
  SADES.06/ANIBACK/EDGE*.SEQ, one per file), 16 are elsewhere, the
  largest single file being ANIMACJE/KADMAR.07/0/UJ23.SEQ with 4. 14530
  elements are anchored.
  (b) THE SECOND ANCHOR IS AUTHORED. Of the anchored ones the words
  f4/f6 hold real values in 13917 cases, zeros in 260+191+142 patterns,
  and the 0x7fff sentinel in 20 - and only 146 elements have f4 == f6 ==
  0, so "no second anchor" is NOT how the game spells an unused field.
  (f4,f6) == (f0,f2) in 7487 (51.5%) - the pair deliberately a no-op -
  and 7043 carry a step: 1455 distinct (dx,dy), magnitude min 1, median
  28, p90 48, max 32767 (the 20 sentinel elements). The most common are
  pure-y: (0,-28) x217, (0,-29) x191, (0,-31) x159, (0,-30) x149,
  (-15,-29) x124. With the engine's `sub [edx+4],(f2-f6)` a negative dy
  moves the position DOWN. w0 is 000f in 14031 elements (shape+art, and
  the f8/fA pair present: 14440 elements carry it, and the lion's frames
  store 32767 there - the value the element initializer 0x41ef0 stamps
  at +8, so the ctor's sentinel is the authored value too).
  (c) WHAT IT IS NOT. Over the 14530 anchored elements: f6 - f2 equals
  the element's own shape row count int16(b17) in 21 cases (0.1%), so
  the second anchor is not the frame's height; f6 equals the bottom row
  int16(b17) - 1 in 2172 (14.95%), within one row in 27.7%, so it is
  not the bottom edge either; and f4 == f0 in 10345 (71.2%), which is
  why most steps are y-only.
  (d) WHAT IT IS: a body line that tracks the pose. Read through the
  authoring that selects these elements - the .MOV scripts are NOT on the
  CD, they are HD-overlay ANIMACJE records (hd_files/ANIMACJE,
  ANIMACJE/<level>/<LEAF>/<SCRIPT>.MOV), and every [STATE] block names
  its art with seq=, which resolves to the CD's ANIMACJE/<level>/<LEAF>/
  <NAME>.SEQ; /tmp/opencode/pr360_states.py resolves them and found 0
  unresolved names for ZARIA.01's seat-line and lion scripts - and
  (f6-f2) is constant within a state and scales across states. For the
  lion's own ZARIA.01 script (LEW.ZAR/LEWPL.MOV, 36 states naming art),
  per state: A_WALK 31..31 over its 12 frames and A_ZABLOK the same,
  A_FIGHT_DOWN 21..25, A_DRAP/A_JUMP_DOWN 28..29, A_WSP_LIN 38..46,
  A_ODLOT a constant 59 over 30 frames, A_KAMIEN 5..33, and A_DEAD 0..56
  - the first frames 55, the last 4, i.e. the distance shrinks as the
  lion collapses. KAT.MOV's 10 frames carry (-6,-21) to (-28,-44);
  PALM.MOV and PALML.MOV, the two ZARIA.01 PALMA scripts, carry
  (-5,-11) to (-5,-5) over their 14 frames.
  (e) ONE ELEMENT, ALL OF IT (/tmp/opencode/pr360_example.py).
  ANIMACJE/ZARIA.01/LEW.ZAR/WALK.SEQ element 0: w0 000f, rows 63, width
  66, f0 44 f2 31 f4 44 f6 62, f8 32767 fA 32767. The draw anchor this
  element is positioned by (ll_seq_anchor_origin, PR-49) is (44,31)
  inside that 66x63 frame; the second anchor is the same x, 31 px lower,
  32 px above the frame's bottom row. 0x42980 on it gives (0,-31): the
  object's live position steps DOWN 31 px on entering the standing state
  and 0x429d0 puts it back. DEATH.SEQ element 0: rows 62, f0 21 f2 6 f4

  (f) WHY THAT IS A PROBLEM, NOT A COMPLETION. The step is applied at
  the same instant PR-354's standing bit flips, it is body-height sized,

- WHY. Two records in a row ended on the same sentence: "whether any
  shipped element carries a second anchor is unmeasured". PR-357 wrote it
  as the honest limit of a machine-code read; PR-359 wrote it as the
  reason not to wire the model. Meanwhile this box had been reporting
  "14 legs ok + 22 named SKIPs" for a week because nothing was staged -
  and LL.iso was sitting in the repository directory the whole time,
  gitignored. So the census is the cheap thing to do, and it is the thing
  F6 needs.

- WHAT THE CENSUS CHANGED IN ME. I expected the second anchor to be a
  rare authored field, because PR-353/PR-354/PR-357 all described landing
  through script commands and level data. It is the opposite: the field
  is authored almost everywhere, and half the elements spell it equal to
  the first anchor - an explicit no-op. That is a grammar fact, not an
  accident: the game's own element initializer stamps 0x7fff at +0, +4
  and +8, the blob then overwrites f0/f2/f4/f6 with real words, and where
  the author wanted no step he wrote the same point twice rather than
  leaving the field alone. So the honest reading of the pair is: the
  engine applies a per-frame offset whenever the author asked for one,
  and for the lion's standing states he asked, every frame, ~31 px.

- THE THREE-WAY CONTRADICTION, STATED PLAINLY (OI-129). The engine
  applies a ~31 px offset at the standing transition. The port does not
  model it. The port matches the original on 69 fixture legs. All three
  cannot be load-bearing: either the covered legs never cross that
  instant (likely - the level legs are short ticks and the lion's
  landing transitions are not among the pinned moments), or the port's
  own ground model lands him at the same coordinates by a different route
  (plausible - PR-352's L15 and the contact model place him from the
  surface, not from his sprite's body line), or the offset is not applied
  where PR-357's chain says it is (which would mean re-reading the call
  site). The deciding measurement is one pose-dump pair at a landing
  instant, and it is written as OI-129 with the recipe in it.

- A NOTE ON THE BOX STATE. Every record since PR-354 reported 14 legs
  because the box was unstaged, and those records are correct for the
  state they ran in. From this PR on the staged configuration is the
  default here, so gates will report the full fixture numbers (69 ok with
  these two gaps named). Anyone comparing counts across records should
  read the box-state sentence, not the count.

- LEDGER NOTE. `tools/jq.py addr 0x42980` and `jq.py oi OI-128` were the
  lookup step again before a single script ran. One vocabulary limit worth
  recording: `jq name` is fed by `doc_census.NAME_RE`, which matches
  `A_*`/`AC_*`/`K_*` state and action names and `.des` keys - C
  identifiers are not names, so `name ll_seq_anchor_land` and
  `name ll_seq_anchor_origin` both return 0 while `free ll_seq_anchor_land`
  finds the records. Function names need either the free-text verb or a
  new vocabulary; nothing in this pass needed more than free text.

- WHY. The layer is now a working step in two sessions' loops. PR-360
  ran `jq.py addr 0x42980` and `jq.py oi OI-128` as its first lookup
  step and reported, in its own record, the one caveat this PR fixes:
  `name ll_seq_anchor_land` and `name ll_seq_anchor_origin` return 0
  while `free ll_seq_anchor_land` returns PR-359 and PR-360. Checked
  live before changing anything: exactly that, and the mechanism as
  PR-360 said - re_db.py feeds name_mentions from doc_census.NAME_RE
  and DES_RE (A_*/AC_*/K_* state and action names, plus .des keys,
  which carry a trailing `=`), so a C identifier is not in the
  vocabulary at all.

- THE FIX IS THE HINT, NOT A VOCABULARY. The split is the same one
  the pinned index and P1/P3 use, so NAME_RE/DES_RE are not touched
  (same rule as ADDR_RE in PR-358: never move the shared acceptance to
  help a client). A new "code symbols" table was considered and
  rejected: record_fts already indexes every record body, so every
  identifier a record names is reachable through free - a second noun
  table with no shared regex behind it is exactly the drift the
  one-parser rule forbids, and would add no row free does not reach.
  What was missing is only that the explicit verb answered a
  non-vocabulary question with a bare "0 records": now a zero-hit
  `name <tok>` whose token matches neither authored shape (A_*/AC_*/K_*
  or `[a-z][a-z0-9_]{3,20}=`) prints a hint saying what names ARE -
  including that .des keys need their trailing `=`, which is how
  `speed=` works and `speed` does not - and points at the free-text
  door. A bare token already auto-routed there, so the auto-path was
  never the trap; only the explicit verb dead-ended silently.

- CONTROL + MUTATION (data-free, runs in seconds). `jq name
  ll_seq_anchor_land` -> 0 records + the hint naming free; same for
  ll_seq_anchor_origin. Negative controls, the vocabulary still
  answers its own nouns with NO hint noise: `jq name A_WALK` -> 15
  records, `jq name speed=` -> 5 records, and a well-shaped token that
  simply has no hits gets no lecture. Regressions from PR-358 all
  hold: `addr 0x33` still hints, bare 0x33 still routes to free,
  `field [obj+0x33]` -> 3 records, `oi OI-129` (PR-360's new row)
  finds its mentions. jq.py's docstring and README now state the
  vocabulary boundary in words, so the hint is not the only place a
  reader learns it.

- THE BOX STATE, SAID PLAINLY. This is the first search-layer PR
  gated with LL.iso staged, so its GATE line carries the real
  fixture-backed counts rather than the deferred caveat PR-355/356/358
  each carried. Those older records stay accurate as written: their
  fixture-free numbers are unchanged by this PR and by the staging,
  and the fixture legs they could not measure are measured now, on
  the same tree this change sits on.

  moves three different things depending on the caller: the live position,
  the ask's aim block, and the snapshot the standing query samples.

  two implementations in the image. 0x53df0 is installed in exactly 31
  tables (0x96c38+0x54 = 0x96c8c for PALMA, 0x96d1c+0x54 for KATAPULT,
  0x96ddc+0x54 for SPLYW and 28 more) and its body is: 0x53e00

  view at 0x96960 is one of its holders (0x96960+0x54 = 0x969b4) - and

  block, after 0x541f6-0x541fd copied the live position into it. So both
  implementations of +0x54 leave [obj+0x89] anchor-shifted, one by doing
  it directly and one by running the ask chain over it. Both paths carry
  the same gate: 0x54218 `test BYTE PTR [ebx+0xb6],0x1` and the +0xbc
  held-surface predicate at 0x5420e/0x54214 skip the chain entirely. So
  the rule, stated once: while the requester holds NO surface, [obj+0x89]
  = position + (f4 - f0, f6 - f2) of the current element; once it holds
  one, the chain does not run. And the standing query measures its first
  clearance exactly there - +0x6c is 0x23a10 `add eax,0x89; ret`
  (PR-349) and 0x45462 passes that to 0x455a0 (PR-348, PR-352 c).
  Through PR-360's numbers, for the lion's ZARIA.01 standing states that

  AUTHORING SENTINEL. 0x53e40 (0x96960+0x50 = 0x969b0; the same value at
  0x979c0, 0xa2268 and the other views) derives a sign by walking
  [obj+0x5c] into [obj+0x50], taking [that], then its own +0x5c/+0x50
  chain, and testing the +0x14 dword of the record it lands on: non-zero
  gives edx = 0xffffffff (0x53e69), zero gives 1 (0x53e70). Then
  0x53e80 takes the CURRENT STATE record's +0x12 word and masks bit 3
  (`and ebx,0x8`), 0x53e83 reads [obj+0x6d], and 0x53e89
  `cmp ecx,0xffffffff`: only when [obj+0x6d] is that sentinel AND the
  state's bit 3 is set does it return the negated sign (0x53e92-0x53e94),
  otherwise the sign itself (0x53e9b). So the sign every anchor site
  except the two class verbs uses comes from the authoring through the
  state record, and [obj+0x6d]'s measured role is a -1 override marker -
  exactly the value 0x53e40 compares, which is what PR-353 saw and read
  as a passed argument.

- WHY. PR-359 ended by refusing to wire the pair for two reasons: the
  engine's argument is the current frame's element, and OI-129 - the port
  is green without the offset. The second reason is the one that could
  actually be wrong, and answering it needed to know WHERE the shift is
  applied. PR-357 had read the method; nobody had read its callers.

- WHAT CHANGED IN MY HEAD. I went looking for a position update and found
  an aim. The pair's position argument is a pointer, and two of its five
  call sites pass not the object at all but a copy - the ask's aim block
  and the snapshot the standing query measures its first clearance at. That
  reorders the whole landing question: the ~31 px is not primarily a step
  the object takes, it is where the engine POINTS the standing query, and
  the object's own position is moved only by the two `ground_on`/`lock2`
  runners of PR-354. That also explains why the port can be green on the
  fixture legs: nothing in them asks a seat question while the lion holds
  no surface, and the port has no snapshot at all.

- THE USEFUL CONSEQUENCE (OI-129, second half, now the nearer one). The
  port's seat_ask_core takes its two points as arguments, so the model is
  not wrong - but the engine's first-test point is never "the position":
  it is the position plus the current element's anchor delta whenever the
  requester holds no surface, and only the bare position when it does. A
  leg that drives ZARIA.01's seat tables with a lion who is NOT on a
  surface therefore has to move the c1 point by (f4 - f0, f6 - f2) - about
  31 px down - to be the ask the engine asks. That is testable with L15
  and L16 already in the tree, and it is the next thing to write.

- WHAT I DELIBERATELY DID NOT CLAIM. The slot counts past +0x8 are
  bounds, and the census's own false positive (0x238ed) is named in the
  record, because the window heuristic is not a proof; three of the six
  leave-shift sites are unread, and 0x5453a looks like a second aim
  chain, which may change paragraph (d)'s "both paths" into "more paths".
  The writer of [obj+0x6d] is still unknown - this pass only read how it
  is read.

  seat_chain_runs (the gate at 0x54200-0x5421f as a boolean),
  seat_sample_direct (0x53df0: copy then shift) and seat_sample_chain
  (0x55070 -> 0x541f0: copy, then shift only if the chain runs) - the new
  leg L17 seat_sample_selftest appended to the ll_mov_selftest chain with
  its forward declaration, and a correction inside L15's comment, which
  carried PR-362's over-general gate sentence. No hook, no return code, no
  Makefile or tool change. Nothing in the port's own step calls any of it:
  the port still has no [obj+0x89] and models no ground_on (PLAN 8g).
HOOKS: L15's seat_ask_core/seat_bracket/seat_slope (PR-352), which L17
  drives, and L16's ll_seq_anchor_land (PR-359), which the two writers

  which is where 0x53df0 and 0x55070 were found and what this leg turns

  contact model places the lion from the surface directly, so the question

  and 124 shift conditionally, which smells like the seat classes keeping

CLOSES: the question PR-362 raised and PR-359 could not answer - does the
  standing query's first sample point carry the anchor offset, or only the
  object's position? It does, in both of the two writers, and the offset
  is the element's second anchor exactly; and for the 124-table path the

CORRECTS: PR-362, twice. Its (d) paragraph says "Both paths carry the
  same gate: 0x54218 ... and the +0xbc held-surface predicate ... skip the
  chain entirely. So the rule, stated once: while the requester holds NO
  surface, [obj+0x89] = position + (f4 - f0, f6 - f2) of the current
  element; once it holds one, the chain does not run." Measured here:
  0x53df0 carries NO test at all - its body is copy, element, sign, shift,
  return - so for the 31 classes that install it (PALMA, KATAPULT, SPLYW)
  the pair is always anchor-shifted. And the 0x541f0 chain has THREE
  tests, not two: 0x54200 `test BYTE PTR [obj+0xb6],0x2` with 0x54207
  `jne 0x54221` makes the `lock2` flag FORCE the chain past both the
  held-surface predicate and the standing test. The 0x55070 half of that
  paragraph is otherwise unchanged. The same sentence in L15's comment,
  in the OI-129 row and in HANDOFF section 8 is corrected in this commit.
  PR-362's census counts and its reading of the pair itself are
  unaffected.
MEASURED: (a) THE TWO WRITERS. Class-table slot +0x54 holds 0x53df0 in
  exactly 31 tables (0x96c38+0x54 = 0x96c8c PALMA, 0x96d1c+0x54 = 0x96d70
  KATAPULT, 0x96ddc+0x54 = 0x96e30 SPLYW and 28 more) and 0x55070 in 124
  (the lion view 0x96960 among them, at 0x969b4) - and those counts are
  counts of SLOTS, not of luck: /tmp/opencode/pr363_slot_census.py reads
  every dword equal to either verb as slot +0x54 of a table based 0x54
  earlier and tests the sibling slots; all 155 pass, uniformly - in every
  one of them +0x48 = 0x23aa0 (PR-351's current-script accessor) and
  +0x50 = 0x53e40 (PR-362's sign getter). The two verbs sit in one and
  the same class-table shape and the split is only in slot +0x54.
  0x53df0: 0x53e00
  `call [view+0x98]`, 0x53e06-0x53e0d copy [obj+0]/[obj+4] into
  [obj+0x89]/[obj+0x8d], 0x53e15 `call [view+0x48]` for the current
  element, 0x53e22 `call [view+0x50]` for the sign, 0x53e27 `mov edx,esi`
  with esi = 0x53dfa's `lea esi,[edx+0x89]`, 0x53e2b `call [edi+0x4]`,
  epilogue. No test of any flag. 0x55070: 0x5507e `call [view+0xb0]` with
  edx = &[obj+0xd6], 0x55084 `lea edx,[ebx+0x89]`, 0x5508c `call 0x541f0`
  - the ask's own aim filler over the same pair - then 0x55096
  `call [view+0x98]`. So the order of the +0x98 call differs as well as
  the gate.
  (b) THE GATE, AS A BOOLEAN. 0x541f0 runs the chain (its
  0x54226/0x54233/0x5423a triple: element, sign, shift on the block it was
  handed) exactly when `([obj+0xb6] & 0x02) || (!held && !([obj+0xb6] &
  0x01))`. The position copy at 0x541f6-0x541fd is unconditional and comes
  FIRST. 0x54200/0x54207 test bit 0x02 and branch straight to the chain -
  PR-354 read that bit as "the extra flag the `2` variants add"; here it
  is the flag that forces the aim chain on for an object that is standing
  and holding a surface. 0x5420e calls +0xbc, which for every lion and
  KAMIEN is 0x23870 `[obj+0xa9] != 0` (PR-350), and 0x54216 skips when it
  answers nonzero; 0x54218/0x5421f skip on bit 0x01.
  (c) LEG L17 (`./ll_level --mov-selftest`, prefix `seat sample:`),
  fixture-free and run in every configuration. Three shape-only elements
  from the L16 blob - element 0 keeps the 0x7fff, element 1 is
  (f0,f2)=(10,20) (f4,f6)=(30,8), element 2 is (10,12)/(10,0) - and 13
  sample-point cases, each with its value taken from the instructions: the
  ungated writer shifts from (890,475) to (890,463) whether or not the
  object holds a surface and whether or not it stands; its x leg gives
  (838,463) facing right and (798,463) facing left from (818,475); a
  0x7fff element leaves the pair at (890,475). The gated writer, free,
  gives the same (890,463); holding a surface keeps (890,475); standing
  keeps it; bit 0x02 with a surface held forces (890,463); bits 0x03 force
  it too; and its x leg mirrors identically, because its sign comes from
  [view+0x50] (0x53e40) rather than from [obj+0x6d].
  (d) WHAT THAT DOES TO THE ASK, WITH NO POSITION EVER CHANGING. The seat
  table (838,463)-(900,463) of L16, asked with its aim at the requester's
  own row (890,475): first clearance measured at the gated writer's pair
  while a surface is held is seat_slope 463 - 475 = -12, so 0x45477/0x4547d
  refuse it. With bit 0x02 set the pair is (890,463), c1 = 0, and the same
  law ANSWERS with the incumbent -12. The x leg alone decides whether a
  pair exists at all: from the requester at (818,475) the shifted sample is
  (838,463) - the table's first record, which the bracket accepts, answer
  with incumbent 0 - facing left it is (798,463), below the first record's
  x, and 0x45393's `jl` gives no bracket. So the ask can be moved across
  the accept boundary without the object moving a pixel, which is the
  difference between L16's route (step the object) and L17's (move the
  point the engine measures).
  (e) EVIDENCE THAT THE MODEL IS THE LAW AND NOT THE TEST. There was no
  red first: the leg passed its first run, because its expected values and
  the model were written from the same instructions. What pins it is
  /tmp/opencode/pr363_mutations.py, five single edits of the model, each
  applied alone and rebuilt: dropping the bit-0x02 force fails 3 cases;
  ignoring the held-surface predicate fails 2; ignoring the standing bit
  fails 1; not applying the shift in the ungated writer fails 7; and
  always passing facing +1 (never mirroring) fails 1. Restored, the
  selftest is rc=0 with no FAILED line.

- WHY. PR-362 had just shown that the engine measures its first clearance
  at a pair somebody else writes, and PR-359 had refused to wire the
  landing step because it could not say what that step was for. L17 is the
  smallest thing that turns that into a claim the port can be wrong about:
  two functions, one boolean, one ask.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. The `lock2` flag. I had the two gates from PR-362 as
  "not standing and not holding", and the first thing I did for this leg
  was read the chain head to the instruction - and 0x54200's test of bit
  0x02 branches straight INTO the chain, over both predicates. So the
  engine's own authoring has a way to keep aiming at the body line while
  standing, and PR-354, which read that bit as the `2` variants' extra
  flag, had no use for it. That is also why the leg tests bit 0x02 with
  and without a held surface: the two mutations that drop either branch
  are caught.

- WHY THE PORT STILL DOES NOT CALL THIS. Nothing in the port fills
  [obj+0x89], because it has no standing query in its step (ground_on,
  ground_off, lock2 and unlock2 are still unmodelled, PLAN 8g). So L17 is
  not a step toward wiring the anchor shift; it is the other half of
  OI-129's question made concrete: if the original's ask is aimed at the
  body line while the lion is free, then the position the ask accepts him
  at is his position PLUS that offset, and a port that places him from the
  surface directly is one body-offset away from the original's number. That
  is a number a pose-dump can show or refute, and OI-129 now says so with
  the exact quantity in it.

- WHY. OI-129's contradiction has a third leg only the provider can
  answer: the ask is aimed at the body line while free (PR-362/363), but
  a STANDING lion is exactly who a seat ask must answer - so what does
  the engine point at then? It points at [obj+0xd6], which is the
  position MINUS the step: the two verbs cancel each other's offset by
  construction, and the difference of the two fields is the delta the
  re-anchor method applies to a position hand-off. That is the whole
  convention F6 would have to port, in three instructions.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. I nearly wrote a phantom function. My first pass
  this session disassembled `dis 0x45300 0x45380` - not an instruction
  boundary - and got a plausible but FALSE function that called 0x4def0
  and a "second ask wrapper" that does not exist; the table rows and
  PR-346's citations disagreed, the skill's discipline says `dis` at the
  boundary is the authority, and re-dis at 0x45320 reproduced the table
  exactly (call 0x541f0 at 0x45340, velocity at 0x45349/0x4534f, call
  0x45400 at 0x4536f). Lesson kept: sweep only from a boundary. The
  provider finding itself came from pairing two slots nobody had joined -
  the +0x54 census of PR-363 and the +0xb0 body of PR-308 were each half
  of a law that only shows up as a difference.

- WHY. PR-364 had left one thread open that mattered for F6: an ask path
  that re-derives a point through the provider and then tests it. It is
  not in the standing query at all, so the seat legs are not affected -
  but the test that does exist is worth knowing: it is the aim-point-plus-
  velocity box test, and on a hit it adds the gap to the box edge into the
  asker's Y velocity. That is a second measured writer of the velocity
  pair, and it belongs to the balloon pickup's helper, not to the ground.
  The other half of the pass matters more for the port: the two families
  of classes disagree about the verbs themselves. The port's L15/L17 model
  is the 155 family; for the other 31 the same slot numbers mean
  something else, and any future port of a 0x53df0-class behaviour must
  not reuse the provider code.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. I corrected a claim I wrote less than an hour
  earlier, and the reason is instructive: I had let the function-list
  entry decide where a body ended. The disassembly says otherwise -
  0x454c6 is a `ret 0x4` and 0x45500 has its own prologue - and once I
  read the body properly its owner turned out to be a completely
  different object, a singleton the balloon class hands out. Two rules
  came out of one mistake: a body's end is its `ret`, and an orphan
  method is worth chasing to its vftable and from there to whoever
  installs it, because that is how an "unreachable" function turns into
  a named class.

- WHY. PLAN 8g lists the +0x58 path as unmodelled, and PR-364 had made it
  look like a mover of the live position for the 155 family. It is that in
  principle, but the only place the engine asks for it is a hand-off
  between two objects that a level line names: a record class resolves a
  named companion at its +0x18, stores it at [obj+0x3c], and then once
  (with a latch it can clear) moves that companion to its own position,
  raises AC_EDGE on it and ORs a packet into its flag block. For the
  ANITAB case that is provably reachable, the verb that runs is the plain
  pair copy, so the anchor delta of PR-364 is not what carries the rider -
  which is exactly the kind of thing the port would get wrong if it wired
  the re-anchor first.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. The verb with the elaborate body - the AC_BUTLA
  raise, the two-sample-point delta, the re-aim - has exactly one caller,
  and the class that caller can be shown to reach implements +0x58 as
  three instructions. Elaborate implementation, minimal use. And the
  position handed across the link is the owner's own pair through +0x90,
  not a computed target: the "placement path" turns out to be "follow me".

- WHY. The F6 thread keeps meeting objects whose kind has to be known:
  the +0xb0 provider of the 155 family, the 31 family's "object getter",
  PR-366's named companion. This pass gives the port the mechanism the
  engine actually uses: an object is asked (verb +0xc) and answers with
  an id, and the caller compares it with a global. The id is shared by
  related classes, so a kind test in the engine is a family test - the
  lion check at 0x24748 accepts four class tables at once. A port that
  compares `[obj+8]` pointers would be stricter than the original and
  would silently break anything that rides, is ridden, or carries.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. The identity getter is not one instruction per
  class: 107 ids for 186 classes, with 30 classes sharing one - so the
  "kind" the engine tests is coarser than the class table, and the
  table set is not the type system. And the same slot +0xb0 is a
  sample-point method in one family and an id getter in the other,
  which is why PR-364's careful reading of 0x544f0 could not be
  generalised - the offset means nothing without the family.

- WHY. The port has to decide what two objects "of the same kind" means
  before it can model riding, carrying or being carried. The engine's own
  test is an id from verb +0xc, and this pass shows the id is not a label
  but a behaviour: everything the engine calls on those objects is the
  same inside an id, and the parts that differ are a short, enumerable
  list of hooks. The second family then says why the 31-family's +0xb0
  companion matters for F6: the classes it names own no position at all -
  their +0x54 and +0x6c are `ret` - so they are carried, they do not
  carry.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That a bare `ret` is a position writer. The engine
  has a whole family of 33 classes whose answer to "write your position"
  is to do nothing, and the standing-query chain treats them like
  anything else. And that the id boundary is exact in one direction only:
  same id, same behaviour, always; same behaviour, many ids. Any port
  that classifies by behaviour will merge what the original keeps apart.

- WHY. This is the other half of F6. PR-349 to PR-365 read how the lion
  measures the surface he stands on; this is what a moving surface keeps for
  itself: its own copy of the x-sorted records, translated whenever it
  moves, bracketed by the same search that the standing query uses, and a
  queue of actions to run when it does. A port that measures every class
  against the level's static array - which is what the port's L15/L17
  legs do - silently gives moving platforms a frozen surface.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the ordering is part of the format. The array is
  kept sorted by x, which is what lets a plain `add` translate it, and it
  is what makes the bracket a binary search in the standing query - so the
  surface data has an invariant the engine depends on, and nothing in the
  port states it.

  answer it differently.

- WHY. The port keeps one surface table per level and measures every object
  against it. The engine hands out shareable record objects instead: the
  header is an object with its own class and kind id, an object built from
  another points at the same records, and whichever one moves translates
  them for every sharer. That is how PR-369's 29 classes can move a surface
  at all - they are not copying terrain, they own a record object the things
  standing on it also point at.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. The header is born empty. A function whose whole body
  is three zeroes and two view stores - so nothing in that path fills an
  array from the level, and whatever fills one is code no record has read
  yet. And the LION's own object carries the header: PR-99 read those three
  constructors and stopped at the view stores, while the very next field,
  [obj+0xee], is a surface-record header.

  0x1f2b5, right after `call 0x53ff0`), so the container is constructed IN
  PLACE at [obj+0xee]: the three words PR-369 called a header are one object
  - its vtable at +0xee, its record array at +0xf2, its count at +0xf6. Four
  sites construct it at [obj+0xa5] instead.
  (b) THE BASE TABLE 0xa0cc0, nine entries: +0x0 0x45230, +0x4 0x39d00,
  +0x8 0x45250, +0xc 0x452d0, +0x10 0x44f90, +0x14 0x453d0, +0x18 0x45320,
  +0x1c 0x45400, +0x20 0x45120. Six of those nine are the functions PR-369
  read as free-standing helpers: the bracket-to-c1 path, the relative ask,
  the standing ask and the filler. None of them has a direct call site except
  0x45320 (6), 0x45400 (1), 0x45120 (5) and 0x44f90 (111) - the rest are
  reached only through a table, which is why the earlier call censuses
  missed them.
  (c) 37 DERIVED SUB-TABLES. Every table in the image whose +0x8 word is
  0x45250: 38, the base plus 37 others. In all 37, exactly three entries
  differ - +0x0, +0x4 and +0x10 - and the six surface entries (+0x8, +0xc,
  +0x14, +0x18, +0x1c, +0x20) are identical to the base; 37 distinct
  functions sit at each of the three overridden slots. The proof that these
  are sub-object tables and not class tables: the derived +0x10 verb at
  0x2b230 begins `sub eax,0xee` - it turns the container pointer back into
  the object base - then `add eax,0xee; call 0x44f90` runs the base
  container's destructor, and `call 0x53a30` runs the outer object's glue,
  with the delete block 0x993ac passed to 0x74bc0 when the flag bit 2 of the
  flags byte is set. Four constructors store one of them directly: 0x29a58
  and 0x2a194 store 0x9a754 at [eax+0xee], 0x29a70 and 0x2a1ac store
  0x99804.
  (d) WHICH CARRY ONE (pr371d_classes.py, a sub-table is a table at
  blob+0xd0..+0x16c whose +0x8 word is 0x45250): 13 of the 29 0x3ddf0
  classes (0x97360, 0x976e0, 0x99718, 0x99828, 0x99a48, 0x99b58, 0x99c68,
  0x9af38, 0x9b048, 0x9e970, 0x9ea80, 0x9fd64, 0x9fe74 - twelve at +0xec,
  0x9ea80 at +0xf4); 11 of the 124 0x55070 classes (at +0xe0, +0xe4, +0xe8,
  +0x128, +0x160; 0x9daf8 is KKULA); 1 of the 31 0x53df0 classes (0x9edd0 at
  +0x144); 3 of the 33 second-family tables (0x9e82c at +0x120, 0x9ee88 at
  +0x144, 0xa0230 at +0x16c). Total 28 of the 219. The LION's class 0x96874
  carries none, which is consistent with PR-369's note that it has no such
  verb.
  (e) THE RECORD FORMAT COMES OUT OF THE PARSER (0x45120; the entry point,
  the four bytes there are 53 51 56 57 = push ebx, ecx, esi, edi): it grows
  the array by one record - `inc edx; imul eax,edx,0xd; add eax,0x4` then
  0x76a64 with the pool ebx=0xa0c64 and 0x76bb7 (0x45149-0x45166) - and per
  record it calls the scanner 0x49920 with "%d" (the string at 0x9182d) and
  with " %c" (0x91830) and the separator test is against ';' (0x3b) and '#'
  (0x23): ';' stores 1 at record+0xc, '#' stores 2, anything else stores 0
  (0x451a1-0x451e0, stored at 0x451be). So a record is {int x, int y, four
  unused bytes, a flag byte} and the level text separates records with ';'
  and '#'.
  (f) THE OTHER TWO FILLERS. 0x45002 copies a container: it takes the source
  count, allocates count*13+4 the same way, and copies each record's +0, +4
  and the +0xc byte (0x45041-0x45053). 0x45070 makes a two-record array from
  queries: it allocates 0x1e (2*13+4), sets the count to 1, then issues
  [0x98278+4] = 0x23ea0 twice and writes the two answers at record 0 and
  record 1 (0x450c5, 0x450d1, 0x450eb, 0x450f2) with both flags set to 1
  (0x450f8, 0x45102). Its only call site is 0x37fa2, inside a constructor
  that installs the views 0x981e8/0x981e0 and then 0x9ef38/0x9ef14/0x9ef0c.
  (g) WHAT THE SURFACE VERBS ANSWER. +0xc (0x452d0) brackets the query x
  with 0x45380 and returns the slope of the segment between the two
  bracketing records, scaled: dy -> `shl eax,5; sub eax,edx` (x31), `lea
  eax,[eax*4]` (x124), `add edx,eax` (x125), `lea edx,[edx*8]` (x1000),
  then `sar edx,0x1f; idiv ebx` over dx (0x452ef-0x45319) - a gradient in
  thousandths, and not the same function as 0x455a0, which
  interpolates and which the port models as seat_slope. +0x8 (0x45250) first
  tests the first record's flag byte against ecx (`movzx edi,BYTE PTR
  [eax+0xc]; cmp edi,ecx; jg` at 0x45258-0x4525e), then takes the FIRST
  record if the query x is left of it or the LAST one otherwise (`imul esi,
  [esi+8],0xd` at 0x45293), copies that record's pair into [edx+0x89] and
  [edx+0x8d] and writes the differences into [edx+0xca] and [edx+0xce]
  (0x4526e-0x452c4) - the same two fields PR-369 saw 0x45320 add to an aim
  before the ask. +0x0 (0x45230) calls the asker's +0x3c verb and, if it
  answers, writes 1 to [ds:0xcef40+0x1c].
  (h) THE LEVEL ARRAY IS THE SAME FORMAT. The code at 0x34871-0x348ff reads
  an array at [esi+0x48] with its count at [esi+0x4c], tests the query
  against the first record and against `imul edx,ebx,0xd` plus the base,
  walks with stride 0xd and stops before the end (`dec eax; imul eax,eax,
  0xd`), then issues a request-block call with the signature 0x98278 - and
  uses 0x98274, the word right before that signature, as a tag at 0x34885.
  Nothing distinguishes the level's array from a container's records.

- WHY. PR-349 to PR-365 read how the lion measures the surface; PR-369 found
  that a moving class keeps its own copy of the records; this is where those
  records come from and who answers questions about them. They are authored
  as text (`%d` then a ';' or '#' separator, with a per-record flag), they
  are attached to objects at construction, and the six verbs that read them
  are shared by every class - only the lifecycle verbs are per-class. So a
  port that measures everything against one level table is not merely
  missing a copy: it is missing a whole object that answers the surface
  questions on behalf of its owner.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the class table and the sub-object table are
  neighbours, and that the boundary between them is what makes PR-368's
  census stop working past +0xdc. Two days of "same-id tables agree at 32
  slots and differ at eleven" were partly a reading of a class's own methods
  next to its members' vtables.

  13 of the 29 0x3ddf0 classes at blob+0xec". The scan read forward from a
  blob and found blocks belonging to the NEXT class. The rule is the other
  way round: a class owns a point list iff a table whose +0x8 word is
  0x45250 sits at its own table address minus 0x24. Measured over the whole
  image there are 38 such blocks; 37 of them have a kind blob starting
  exactly 0x24 later and one - 0xa0cc0, the base table - belongs to no
  class. So 37 classes own a point-list verb block: 29 of the 29 0x3ddf0
  classes, 2 of the 31 0x53df0 ones, 5 of the 33 second-family tables, 1
  whose +0x54 is 0x2b1a0, and 0 of the 124 0x55070 ones. Named classes
  among them: KTRASA (0x9dbfc) and TUNTRAS (0x9f7b4). My "0x9daf8 = KKULA
  is one" is wrong: the block I found at KKULA+0xe0 belongs to KTRASA, whose
  table starts 0x24 after that block.
  (2) PR-371 (c) implied the derived tables are separate tables attached to
  the container. They are the nine dwords immediately below the class's own
  method array - the container's vtable word IS that prefix (0x29a58 stores
  0x9a754 at [obj+0xee], and 0x9a754+0x24 = 0x9a778 is the class array the
  same function stores at [obj+0x8]) - and PR-371's derived-table count of
  37 is the number of owning classes, which is consistent but was not
  understood as such.
  (3) PR-371 and OI-128 said the container sits at [obj+0xee]. Not always:
  the verbs are handed containers at +0xee, +0xa5, +0x44 and once +0x106.
  What is universal is that the argument is the ADDRESS of the field - every
  site uses `lea reg,[obj+off]` or `add reg,off` and none loads a pointer -
  so the container is embedded in all of them and only the offset varies.
  (4) PR-370 wrote that the base part "installs the view pair
  0xa23b8/0xa23b0 at +8/+0xc", and PR-99 called the same shape a two-view
  idiom: it is one array installed twice. 0xa23b0 = 0xa23b8-8.
  Method point: PR-371's census that matched an indirect call to any mention
  of a field within 0x60 bytes over-counts, because the object's dispatch
  array is itself at [obj+0x8]. 0x28e96 is the counterexample:
  `mov esi,[eax+0x8]; call [esi+0x8]` there is a class method call
  (0x9a674's +0x8 is 0x23e00), not a container verb. Only direct calls to a
  verb count, and they are few: 0x44fe0 63, 0x45200 10, 0x45320 6, 0x45120
  5, 0x45400 1.

  other 10 store non-tables, and one of those forms is the request-block

  addressed three times: the class's verbs at array+0, the container's verbs
  at array-0x24 (nine slots), and the second base at array-0x2c, which is
  the container's block minus one slot. A call at [obj+0xc]+0x10 and a call
  on the container at +0x8 therefore reach the same function 0x45250. The
  same function also clears [eax+0x126] and [eax+0x12a] and writes the
  request-block signature 0x98278 at [eax+0x12e].

  29 of the 0x3ddf0 family, 2

  Not one of the 124 0x55070 classes owns one, which is PR-368's split seen

- WHY. PR-371 said the port is missing the object that answers surface
  questions for its owner. This says who has one and how it is attached: 37
  classes, every one of the 0x3ddf0 family and eight others, carrying the
  container's nine verbs as a prefix of their own method array and the
  container itself inline at an offset of their own choosing. The 124
  classes of the 0x55070 family have no such thing and answer only from the
  level's records - which is exactly what the port models.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That my own forward scan had the ownership backwards:
  the block I read as "inside a class blob at +0xec" belongs to the class
  whose table starts 0x24 later, and correcting that turns "13 of 29" into
  "all 29", which makes the two-writer split of PR-368 an ownership law
  rather than a behaviour difference.

- WHY. The port has no notion of an object answering surface questions for
  itself, and PR-372 showed which 37 classes do. This is the code that
  makes it true at run time: the constructor hands the object three
  pointers into one method array - its own verbs, the container's verbs one
  slot under the second base, and the container itself inline - and the
  container's verb table is the class's own, not the shared one. A port
  that models one dispatch path and one shared surface table is not just
  missing data; it is missing the mechanism.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the same two fields ([obj+0x8], [obj+0xc]) hold
  a different relationship depending on whether the class owns a point
  list, and that I had measured that relationship an hour earlier and read
  it backwards because I matched instruction forms instead of values.

  exactly three entries differ - +0x0, +0x4 and +0x10": measured slot by
  slot it is +0x10 in all 37, +0x4 in 36 and +0x0 in 32; the five blocks
  that keep the base +0x0 are 0x9dbd8, 0x9ef14, 0x9f790, 0xa1f6c and
  0xa2030 - exactly the five second-family owners PR-373 listed - and only
  0x9ef14 keeps +0x4. So the count of distinct per-class functions is 32
  at +0x0, 36 at +0x4 and 37 at +0x10, not 37 everywhere. (2) I called
  them "derived sub-tables" and "the container's method table": they are
  blocks inside the owner's own method array (PR-372, PR-373), and calling
  them sub-tables is what made PR-371's ownership count wrong.

  +0x8 0x45250, +0xc 0x452d0, +0x14 0x453d0, +0x18 0x45320, +0x1c 0x45400
  and +0x20 0x45120 hold the SAME dwords as the base 0xa0cc0 in all 37,
  and nothing else in the block is ever a surface verb. Only +0x0, +0x4
  and +0x10 vary (32, 36, 37 of the 37).
  (b) THE +0x10 HOOK, UNIFORM IN ALL 37 (pr374b_thunks.py, class 0x96c38
  at 0x20760): `push ebx; push ecx; mov ecx,edx; sub eax,0xa5; mov ebx,eax;
  test cl,4; je ...; mov edx,0x96560; call 0x74bc0; call 0x74be0; ...`
  then `mov edx,1; add eax,0xa5; call 0x44f90; ...; call 0x53a30;
  test cl,2; ... call 0x5c370`. The this-pointer is the CONTAINER (that is
  why it subtracts the class's container field, 0xa5 here and 0xee in
  0x2b230); it optionally prints with the class's descriptor block, runs
  the base container destructor 0x44f90, then the outer object's glue
  0x53a30, and frees. That is a destructor, in the slot the base table
  fills with 0x44f90.
  (c) THE +0x0 AND +0x4 HOOKS FORWARD INTO THE CLASS. For 0x96c38 they are
  one instruction each: 0x207d0 `call 0x1e540; ret` and 0x207c0
  `call 0x1e560; ret` - PR-340's element region. For the 0x3ddf0 family
  they call 0x3df50 and, at +0x4, 0x3df90 then 0x3df50; 0x3df50 reads a
  value (0x749a0, then 0x49580) and stores it at [obj+0x112]. So these
  are load/construct hooks, and the class body they jump to is the element
  code - the same region whose methods translate the container at +0xa5.
  (d) THE TWO SLOTS BELOW THE BLOCK USE [obj+0xc] AS THIS. Every one of
  the 37 blocks is preceded by two per-class functions; for 0x96c38 those
  are 0x20750 (which only returns) and 0x206f0, which opens
  `sub eax,0xc` - recovering the object from an argument that arrived as
  obj+0xc - and ends `add eax,0xa5; call 0x44f90; sub eax,0xa5; call
  0x53a30; ... call 0x5c370`: the object's destructor reached through the
  second base. So [obj+0xc] is a real interface with its own thunks and
  its own this convention, and the container's nine verbs are that
  interface's slots +0x8..+0x24. The base table 0xa0cc0 has no such pair:
  the two dwords before it are 0x23ea0 and 0x23e00, request-block verbs
  (0x23ea0 is `mov [eax],edx; mov [eax+4],ebx; ret`, the pair writer
  PR-369 called [0x98278+4]), i.e. whatever array precedes it, not a
  class's.

- WHY. The F6 thread has been asking what the engine measures a moving
  object against. This says what is and is not per-class about that
  measurement: the ask, the slope, the bracket, the relative ask, the
  standing ask and the text parser are one shared implementation in all 37
  owners and the base, and what each class supplies is only how its point
  list is created, filled and destroyed. A port may therefore treat the
  surface verbs as one mechanism, and must treat the container's lifecycle
  as the per-class part.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the "derived" tables I had been counting were
  not tables of a sub-object at all but ordinary stretches of the owner's
  method array, and that the strongest evidence for it was a `sub eax,0xc`
  in a destructor - a function that knows it was called with the object's
  second interface pointer.

- WHY. The F6 thread has been chasing the difference between measuring the
  level's surface and measuring one's own. Here is the authored origin of
  that difference: the same load hook that fills an object's point list
  also puts its first authored point into the fields the standing second
  query adds. The two halves PR-369 found - the extra pass and the record
  array - are one authored feature. And the surface query is not private
  to the asker: the writer translates through its own container and then
  asks the companion through the companion's verbs, which is how a pair of
  authored objects keeps one standing on the other's surface.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That I had called a flag-setter a text reader because
  I read past a `ret`. The bounded-body rule is the same one that caught
  the PR-372 offset mistake: reading a window instead of a function.

  (`mov eax,1; ret` or `xor eax,eax; ret` on a flag in eax);
  `mov ecx,[edx+0x8]; mov eax,edx; call [ecx+0x3c]` - ask the CANDIDATE
  whether it is askable; if that fails, set bit 0x40 of the byte at
  [obj+0x66]; if it passes, `call 0x1f590` and on success set bit 0x80 of
  that same byte; then `mov eax,ebx; call 0x3df50` either way. The other
  wrapper at 0x1f6f0 branches to three sites that OR 0x40, 0x80 or 0x1
  (at [obj+0x67]) and then calls 0x3df50; 0x27626 and 0x34623 guard the
  same way.
  (d) THE GUARD IS NOT NEW TO THIS ENGINE - IT IS ALSO IN THE STANDING
  QUERY. 0x1f372 does `mov edx,[eax+0x112]; test edx,edx; mov ecx,
  [edx+0x8]; mov eax,edx; call [ecx+0x3c]; test eax,eax` and only
  continues for [obj+0x5c] == 6, reading a per-kind array at [obj+0x50];
  and the wrapper at 0x1f43a tests `[obj+0x5c] == 9`, sets bit 0x40 of
  [obj+0x66] and calls PR-337's 0x3df00 before linking. So the same
  askable verb guards both linking a companion and asking it.
  (e) THE FIELD ITSELF: 61 instruction rows name [reg+0x112] - 16 stores,
  27 loads and 14 compares (10 of them `cmp [reg+0x112],0`), counted on
  the operand shape (pr376_link.py); the stores are at
  0x1e1db, 0x2401d, 0x2709b, 0x2c10b, 0x2e04b, 0x33ced, 0x362bb, 0x39edb,
  0x3b2ad, 0x4d6c5, 0x500fd, 0x3df83, 0x3e042, 0x3dd28, 0x285d7
  (`mov [esi+0x112],1` - a flag, not a pointer) and 0x283c9.

```

- WHY. The F6 thread wants to know what an authored object stands on when
  it is not standing on the level. PR-375 showed it asks a companion; this
  shows the engine refuses to link a companion that cannot answer a
  surface question, and that the 37 classes with authored point lists are
  never themselves answerable. The two halves of the mechanism - the
  askable test from PR-322 and the point-list ownership law from
  PR-372/PR-373 - are complementary sets in every measurement taken here.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the "unknown" verbs I opened PR-376 to read were
  two the ledger has known for fifty records, and that the count 204/15
  says the askable answer is a constant written into the table: the engine
  never computes whether something can be asked, the author decided it.

- WHY. The port asks every object the same surface question and lets every
  object be asked. The original decides both per class: 64 tables opt in to
  accepting a companion, 15 agree to be asked, and the two sets barely
  overlap. If the port is to reproduce which object stands on which, it
  needs these two per-class flags, not a rule derived from the level.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That six of the classes the F6 thread cares most
  about - KTRASA, the two element-region classes, and three others with
  authored point lists - have no way to accept a companion at all, while
  twenty ordinary 0x55070 classes do.

- WHY. The port reads a handful of property lines and stops its walk at
  one. The engine has a closed set of 14 named keys plus the point-list
  grammar, read by one scanner through one cursor, and every key has a
  compiled default. That is the difference between "an object authored
  with a patrol and damage" and "an object authored with a patrol,
  damage, spawn point, hit time, eight coefficient floats, a control word
  and a companion rate".

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the defaults are not zero sentinels but named
  floats written at the call site - 0.6, 0.02, 0.12, 0.08, 0.06, 0.04,
  0.02, 0.01 - and that the `F` key I had been chasing for three records
  is one ordinary entry in a fifteen-key list.

  (c) THE GRAMMAR AND THE FACTORY INTERLEAVE. The ` id = %d ` and
  ` spawn = %d , %d ` segment at 0x34332 sits in the same address region
  as the KPAJECZ/KKULA/KTRASA compares (0x35049-0x350bd), and the
  `F`-chain call sites are scattered through the same code
  (0x34477, 0x346a6, 0x3b506, 0x3b6d6). Reading a record is therefore
  one pass of factory code: choose the class by its token, build the
  object, then run the shared property segments over the same cursor.
  (d) THE ` id = `/` spawn = ` SEGMENT, IN ORDER. 0x34332: scan
  ` id = %d ` into [arg+0x12e] (default 0 if unmatched); if that id is
  0 the rest is skipped; otherwise scan ` spawn = %d , %d ` into
  [arg+0x136]/[arg+0x13a] (the scan receives `lea ebx,[arg+0x136]` as
  its out-buffer base) and then compare [ebx+8] with [ebx+0xc].
  [arg+0x12e] is the same field PR-376's and PR-377's records show
  holding a kind-table pointer in other objects, so this id field is a
  second use of one offset - recorded, not resolved.

```

- WHY. The port stops its record walk at a property line and treats the
  keys it knows as properties of the object being built. The original has
  no per-class property readers at all: one shared sequence reads the
  record, and the class is chosen by one token compare in that same
  sequence. That is why the same 14 keys appear everywhere - and it tells
  the port that its property handling belongs to the record reader, not
  to a per-class hook.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the class of an authored object is decided by
  exactly one string compare per class, twelve of which this pass located
  for the first time, sitting in the same code as the property readers.

- WHY. The port knows the authored class names from the level files and
  maps a handful of them. The original's mapping is 166 tokens naming 157
  of its 219 classes, with every point-list-owning class named, and the
  classes the port has never seen a name for are mostly named too. It
  also settles what the port's property handling should attach to: in the
  original, reading properties is a class verb - the code is shared, but
  every class decides whether and where it is reachable.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That I had been reading the same factory for three
  records and had extracted 12 of its 166 branches; and that the seven
  classes allowed to be asked a question are the seven whose authored name
  begins 'TLew', which is the group-object prefix the level files use.

- WHY. The port implements one "read the object's text" step. The
  original has a two-slot chain per class (+0x78 entry, +0x9c
  continuation), and the entry asks the class whether it takes a
  companion and, for the askable classes, asks a second question with the
  authored placement damage as its argument. Naming those slots is what
  lets the port put its own load step in the right place.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the most-dispatched class verb in the whole
  engine is the one that returns a facing word (215 sites), while the
  load verb - the one that turns authored text into an object - is
  dispatched at four sites and otherwise reached by direct call.

- WHY. The port builds an object and parses its record in one go. The
  original separates them: the class-name factory only constructs, and a
  request handler - which already holds the record text - drives the load
  verb, copies back a 13-byte result and only then asks the object a
  question. That is why the same property readers serve every class and
  why the load verb has a per-class continuation: the request is
  class-independent, the reading is not.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That a handler sets bit 0x40 of the link byte at
  [obj+0x66] before the load call, so the companion bookkeeping of
  PR-376 is partly done by the request, not by the class.

- WHY. The port has no notion of "this object is willing to be linked to
  another"; PR-377 found the switch and this record shows which way it
  points: the question is put to the companion's own class, so being
  linkable is a property of being the kind of thing that can be linked,
  not of the object that initiates. That is the shape the port's
  companion handling has to take.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the request handlers double as load verbs: the
  engine does not have a separate loader entry point per class, it has
  one verb slot that the request happens to call.

  call 0x749a0`, then for slot [container+ecx*4]: iterates i <

  object's chain at [obj+0x34]. Per candidate: `call [cand class
  +0x60]`, skip if zero; require [cand+0x24] == [requester+0x24]
  unless a further argument is non-zero; skip the requester itself;
  `call DWORD PTR [cand class+0x78]` with eax = candidate, edx = a

  first non-empty answer.

- WHY. The port's ask path is built on the vocabulary of PR-244 and
  PR-249 ("the requester's ask walk 0x4b500", "the answer entry
  [obj.vt+0x78]"). If my last four records' name for that slot reached
  the port, the port would gain a second, wrong model of the same
  mechanism. Two concrete facts are worth keeping from this walk: the
  layer equality is [obj+0x24] and the candidate filter reads
  [obj+0x2c]; and the CHECK_LEW channel stops at the first non-empty
  answer while the other channels merge them all.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That I had walked this path before. The port
  cites 0x4b500 -> [obj.vt+0x78] = 0x552e0 -> 0x55230 in a comment
  written in PR-90, and I re-derived it four records later under a
  different name - a reminder to query the index for the slot before
  naming it.

  +0x60 holds the default 0x23b80 (`mov eax,[obj+0x2c]; ret`) in 178
  and 32 distinct other addresses in the remaining 41. Reading all 32:
  37 of the 41 tables are `mov eax,1; ret` stubs (0x22d10, 0x23280,
  0x26000, 0x26310, 0x26330, 0x26350, 0x26e10, 0x2db70, 0x2f730,
  0x2fb00, 0x30720, 0x30950, 0x31c00, 0x339d0, 0x339f0, 0x33a10,
  0x35d50, 0x35df0, 0x35e10, 0x35e40, 0x35e90, 0x35eb0, 0x36170,
  0x3ab70, 0x3aba0, 0x3b770, 0x3baa0, 0x4fca0), and four test
  something. Method note: five of those stubs (0x2f730, 0x30720,
  0x30950, 0x3b770, 0x3baa0) have no row in the `insn` table at their
  own address - the index's linear sweep left a gap - and read only
  through `leodb.py dis`, which shows `mov eax,0x1; ret` at each.
  (b) THE FOUR THAT TEST SOMETHING. 0x260b0 (KROPLAS) and 0x26110
  (KROPLA) call 0x52d30 for the position of [[0xcef40]+0x394] - the
  same level member PR-244 named as the no-candidate fallback - and for
  their own, take the absolute difference of the first word with the
  `cdq/xor/sub` idiom and answer only if it is below 100
  (`cmp eax,0x64; setl al`). 0x24bb0 (PILAGEN) calls that member's
  +0x68 verb, which returns a point, and answers only if that point
  lies inside its own rectangle at [obj+0xf2] - x between [edx] and
  [edx+8], y between [edx+4] and [edx+12]; it also puts the data
  address 0x98278 in the third slot of its query buffer at 0x24bd2.
  0x339a0 (PIOR_RAN) answers only when the signed word at [obj+0x1ba9]
  is not negative.

  pr380m_pairs.tsv (the earlier scripts read its second column, which is
  the token's compare site, not the class table - a method note worth

  (two tables), TUNTRAS, TRASA, TRASA2, 0x9e294 - all take the
  always-allow 0x36170; the machinery group 0x35d50-0x35eb0 is one

  TWINDA, GEJZER, GORYL, KLODA, DEMOTEXT, PILARYB, GPTAK_RA) and 5
  tables no token names. The F6 classes are NOT among them: LION
  0x96874, KAMIEN 0x96a88, DRABINKA 0x97cdc and the shared animal class
  0x97f64 all keep the default contact-node filter.
  (d) WHAT THE DEFAULT FILTER DECIDES. [obj+0x2c] is written from the
  class's +0x8 verb at 0x1eb92-0x1eb9a (`mov ecx,[obj+8]; call
  DWORD PTR [ecx+0x8]; mov [obj+0x2c],eax`), and 204 of the 219 class
  tables install 0x23e00 at +0x8: a point-in-rectangle test - the point
  at [eax]/[eax+4] against the rectangle at [edx], [edx+8], [edx+4],
  [edx+12] - returning 0 or 1. So an object passes the ask walk's
  filter exactly while a shape meet has been recorded in it, which is
  the same condition the port states for the answer chain ("that needs
  a real shape meet (0x53ae0)", ll_level.c 6560).
GATE: light: verify-index verify-docs rc=0 (ok); nothing under ported/
  is touched by this record, so the build and level gates were not run;
  the index was regenerated with this record in the tree before the
  run.
```

- WHY. The ask path in the port filters candidates by plane and by
  contact, and this record shows the engine's split of that work: the
  plane rule is one comparison in the walk (0x4b5a1, [obj+0x24]), the
  contact rule is a class verb (+0x60, and 178 classes take the
  standard one). If the port ever needs a class that answers without
  contact, the original's own example is the road group, which installs
  the always-allow stub.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the 41 exceptions are almost all "always
  answer" rather than "never", and that the always-answer group is the
  roads, the machine group and props - the things an ask would
  otherwise exclude by contact - while the lion and the animals keep the
  contact requirement.

  holds 0x23ed0 (tests bit 0x4 of dl, then calls 0x74bc0 and 0x74be0
  with edx = 0x96858), 0x9827c holds 0x23ea0 (`mov [eax],edx; mov

  (d) A BOUNDS CHECK ON MY OWN CENSUSES. 157 of the 219 tables in the

```

- WHY. The port keeps an object's authored points as a plain array. The
  original gives every point its own 12-byte object whose class is a
  three-slot tail of the owner's own class table - so a point is an
  object with verbs, and the owner, its element class and the owner's
  authored numbers are one contiguous block. Knowing the element class
  is a table tail is what makes the 0x98274/0x98278 pair readable in
  any other class: look at the last slots of the owner's table.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That I spent an afternoon on a pair of addresses
  the ledger has cited in 45 and 73 records. The index entry for an
  address is the first thing to read, not the last.

CORRECTS: PR-386, twice, both about the same bytes. It said "0x98284 onward
  is packed non-pointer data (0x74bac00, 0x255d000, 0xee00, ...)" and called

  verb". The bytes are a descriptor array that starts at 0x98285, one byte
  before that read: the dword at 0x98284 is 0x74bac00 only because the whole
  array is misaligned by one byte, and 0x74bac is a real pointer. Also a
  method note on this pass: my first script used field offsets one dword off
  from the record base and reported 376 records; the corrected rule gives
  243, and the numbers below are from the corrected script.
MEASURED: (a) THE SHAPE (pr387_desc3.py). Records are 20 bytes at stride
  0x14 and every one sits at 1 mod 4 - the arrays as a whole are misaligned
  by one byte, which is why PR-356 saw "blocks at 1 mod 4" and why the
  index finds 0x74bac only in unaligned dword windows. 243 records have all
  five fields well-formed with 0x74bac in the second field, in 72 arrays
  (longest 23 records), spanning 0x9637d-0xa6b7d and interleaved with the
  class tables; relaxing the rule to the shape alone gives 288 records,
  which is the 281 PR-356 counted. No class table holds 0x74bac in any of
  its slots (0 of 219), and none of the 243 records sits at a class-table
  start, so the arrays are not vtables and are not the tables themselves.
  (b) THE STUB. 0x74bac is `push edx; mov edx,1; mov eax,0x95c40; call
  0x77bdc; pop edx; ret` and 0x95c40 is the runtime string "undefined
  constructor or destructor called!". The pure-virtual stub is a different
  function: 0x74980 loads 0x95c20 "pure virtual function called!". So the
  fields around 0x74bac are constructor/destructor slots and the stub marks
  the ones a class does not define - 243 records carry it in the second
  field and 39 in the first (a class with no constructor).
  (c) WHAT THE FIELDS DO. The first field is the class's constructor:
  walking its code to the first `ret` finds a `mov [reg+8],T` for a known
  class table, for 137 of the 219 tables. The third field is a member
  function that equals the first dword of a class table - the class's vtable
  slot 0 - for 197 of the 219. The two fields name the SAME class for 134
  of the classes and disagree for 3; together they reach 200 of the 219, and
  19 have no descriptor at all (11 of them token-named, including the shared
  road class 0x9e294, and 8 token-unnamed, including LION 0x96874). For 54 of
  the 62 token-unnamed class tables this is the only handle on them: the
  descriptor gives the ctor (0x1e0a0, 0x27030, 0x39c40, 0x63750, 0x71860,
  ...) and the identity. Worked example: the record at 0x99501 holds
  {0x27030, 0x74bac, 0x27420, 0x12c, 0} - 0x27030 installs the class table
  0x9a54c at [obj+8] and 0x27420 is 0x9a54c's own first slot.
  (d) THE FOURTH FIELD IS THE OBJECT SIZE, AND IT AGREES WITH PR-380. For
  all 144 classes where both routes exist, the descriptor's fourth field
  equals the byte count PR-380 read in the token branch's `mov eax,size;
  call 0x5c320`: 144 of 144, no exception. Two independent readings of the
  compiled image, one from code and one from data, give the same object
  size - the earlier draft of this pass reported 102 of 103 only because of
  the off-by-one in (a).
  (e) THE ARRAY BESIDE THE POINT-LIST CLASS (corrects PR-386). The bytes
  after the point-list verbs at 0x98280 are the array at 0x98285:
  {0x74bac, 0x255d0, 0x25540, 0xee, 0} at 0x98285, {0x24110, 0x74bac,
  0x255f0, 0x14a, 0} at 0x98299, and so on to the record at 0x98311
  {0x26060, 0x259b0, 0x25970, 0xfa, 0}. That is the block OI-128 mentions:
  0x25970 is its third field, and its body ends with `mov edx,0x98310; call
  0x74bc0` - the same call the ctors make at 0x2028b with 0x964c0 and the
  point class's own verb at 0x23ed0 makes with 0x96858, always the record
  address minus one. 0x74bc0 puts that argument in ebx and never reads it.
GATE: light: verify-index verify-docs rc=0 (ok); nothing under ported/ is
  touched by this record, so the build and level gates were not run; the
  index was regenerated with this record in the tree before the run.
```

- WHY. The port has to be told which class each scenario object is and how
  big its record is; until now that came only from the name-compare factory.
  The original carries the same information as data, one descriptor per
  class, and for 54 classes it is the only copy. It also settles a question
  about the tables themselves: a descriptor's third field is the class's
  vtable slot 0, and it matches the table start that PR-380 derived from the
  ctor rule for 197 of 219 tables - so the table boundaries used since then
  are the real ones.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the odd 1-mod-4 alignment PR-356 noticed was not
  noise but the signature of a whole misaligned array, and that the value
  repeated through it, which I had already used as junk twice, is a runtime
  stub with a printed message that says what the field means.

  hold the same +0x60 filter 0x36170 (`mov eax,1; ret` - every candidate
  passes), the same +0x78 answer verb 0x3f010, and a this-adjusted
  destructor thunk at +0x9c. A road never answers: 0x3f010 writes a zeroed
  12-byte record with the flag byte at +0xc cleared into the buffer the
  asker handed in; the only thing it does is, when the requester in ebx
  equals [obj+0x3c], clear its own container at [obj+0x44] through 0x45320
  first. So the road is a candidate that always passes and never replies,
  and what makes it interesting is not its answer but the container it
  drops and the point list 0x3f0f0 builds beside it.
CORRECTS: PR-384's name for the slot. "Per-class filter" describes what the
  call site does with the return value, but the slot is where the class's
  destructor lives: 181 tables hold one shared two-instruction placeholder
  0x23a40, and 7 hold a destructor thunk with the compiler's flag protocol
  (`test cl,0x4` or `test bl,0x4` -> release and free, `test cl,0x2` ->
  0x53a30 then free). No measured behaviour changes - the placeholder really
  does always return 1 - but the 7 exceptions are not predicates, and the
  four that are this-adjusted (`sub eax,0xc`) are exactly the road family,
  which PR-385 had picked out for a different reason. PR-387's "nothing in
  the image reads these arrays" is also too strong: each of those 7
  destructors passes its own descriptor record to 0x74bc0, which is the
  first live use of the arrays found.
MEASURED: (a) THE CENSUS (pr388_dtor3.py, all 219 tables). At +0x9c: 181
  tables hold 0x23a40 = `mov eax,1; ret` - one address, not 181 different
  always-true functions; 7 hold a function with the destructor protocol; 31
  hold something else, and two of those are the out-of-bounds reads PR-386
  and PR-387 predicted (0x981e8 reads back 0x74bac00 and the shared road
  class 0x9e294 reads 0x38a8000, both shifted words of the descriptor array
  that follows the table). (b) THE 7 THUNKS. 0x35a10 (KTRASA), 0x3a7d0
  (TUNTRAS), 0x4f8d0 (TRASA) and 0x4fa40 (TRASA2) all open with
  `mov ecx,edx` (or `mov ebx,edx`) and `sub eax,0xc` and all end by
  returning obj-0xc; 0x20760 (KILOF_PL 0x96b88), 0x29e90 (SCHODY4/BRECT
  0x99668) and 0x39950 (the no-token class 0x9ee88) have the same flag
  protocol without the -0xc adjust. Each of the seven loads a constant and
  calls 0x74bc0 then 0x74be0: 0x96560, 0x99398, 0x9d64c, 0x9e418, 0x9f4d4,
  0xa1498 and 0xa14ac, and every one of those is one byte before a record
  of a PR-387 descriptor array (0x96561, 0x99399, 0x9d64d ... are 1 mod 4).
  (c) WHAT THE CALLEE DOES. 0x74be0 is `jmp 0x5c370`, i.e. operator delete;
  0x74bc0 takes the object in eax, reads the allocation header at [eax-4]
  and calls 0x76c00 with it, returning eax-4, and it puts the descriptor
  argument in ebx and never reads it. The other branch calls 0x53a30 with
  edx=1 and then `test cl,0x2; call 0x5c370` - free only when that flag
  bit is set. (d) THE CALL SITES. `mov ebx,[obj+8]; mov edx,asker;
  mov eax,obj; call DWORD PTR [ebx+0x9c]; test eax,eax; je bail` appears
  exactly 5 times, at 0x3d9d7, 0x3e8bd, 0x50fdb, 0x53ccd (inside the
  0x53c90 answer verb) and 0x55318 (inside 0x552e0, the answer verb of 78
  tables). All five sit after the same prologue: build the 12-byte answer
  record on the stack with 0x749a0, call 0x53ae0 (eax=me, edx=the requester)
  and bail if it returns 0, then this [T+0x9c] call, then the class's own
  work, then `repnz movsd` of 12 bytes into the caller's buffer with the
  flag byte moved to record+0xc - the answer format of PR-384. (e) THE ROAD
  ANSWER. 0x3f010: `push ecx; sub esp,8; mov [esp],edx` (keep the answer
  buffer), `mov edx,ebx; cmp edx,[eax+0x3c]` - if the requester equals
  [obj+0x3c] then `mov ebx,2; add eax,0x44; xor ecx,ecx; call 0x45320`,
  the container clear of PR-381; then fill the answer buffer with 12 zero
  bytes through 0x749a0 and clear its flag byte: `mov BYTE PTR [eax+0xc],
  0`. The neighbouring 0x3f0f0 is the road's own initializer - it parses the
  point list into [obj+0xa5] with 0x44f10, makes the 12-byte elements of
  class 0x98278, offsets them by [obj] and [obj+4], and hands the block to
  0x4a0b0.
GATE: light: verify-index verify-docs rc=0 (ok); nothing under ported/ is
  touched by this record, so the build and level gates were not run; the
  index was regenerated with this record in the tree before the run.
```

- WHY. The F6 thread needs to know what happens when the lion asks what is
  under him. This says the road classes are not answering: they pass every
  filter, return an empty record, and the only road-specific work in that
  path is in the destructor thunk - which is also the only place the engine
  provably touches its own class-descriptor records. So the "surface" the
  lion stands on is carried by the point-list containers (0x3f0f0,
  [obj+0xa5], the 0x98278 element class), not by the answer verbs.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the four this-adjusted thunks are exactly the four
  road tables, and that the free branch of a destructor sits on the ask
  path - the engine calls it as a predicate and lets the requester's address
  bits decide whether memory is released.

MEASURED: (a) THE GATE'S SHAPE (pr389_53ae0.py). 0x53ae0 (eax=the answering
  object, edx=the requester) makes exactly these calls: 0x53030 once,
  `[T+0x44]` twice - once on the answerer at 0x53b18 and once on the
  requester at 0x53b2b - `[T+0x10]` twice on the requester, 0x52b10 twice,
  0x749a0 twice (the 12-byte answer record of PR-384) and 0x49580 once
  (the OR-merge). It bails if 0x53030 reports no pair, then requires of the
  answerer's row-flag word `test ah,0x4` (bit 0x1000) and
  `and eax,0x40400; cmp eax,0x40400` (bits 0x400 and 0x40000 both set),
  and of the requester's that bit 0x10000 is clear. The two records it
  emits are built by 0x749a0 with the flag byte at +0xc forced to 1
  (`or dl,0x1` at 0x53bcc, copied out with four `movs` to the caller) and
  to 2 (`or bl,0x2` at 0x53c36, merged through 0x49580) - the AC_BLOK and
  AC_BLOK_Y answers of PR-238; the choice between the two branches is
  `and ecx,0x20400; cmp ecx,0x20400` at 0x53bd7. One thing to flag rather
  than claim: these answer records have the same 13-byte shape as PR-335's
  authored surface-table records at [obj+0xa5] (class 0x98278) - four
  dwords and a flag byte at +0xc - and PR-335's separator ';' writes 1 and
  '#' writes 2 there, the same two values 0x53ae0 forces. Whether the two
  flag bytes mean the same thing is open.
  (b) THE PAIR TEST 0x53030 (pr389_gate.py). It opens with
  `mov eax,[eax+0x24]; cmp eax,[edx+0x24]` - the plane words of PR-385. If
  they are EQUAL it takes 0x530dc: `call [T+0x4c]` on the requester and on
  the answerer, which return a 4-dword box, and it tests the classic
  rectangle overlap (x1 <= X2, X1 >= x2, y1 <= Y2, Y1 >= y2). If the planes
  DIFFER it calls 0x52dc0 on each object instead: 0x52dc0 calls the same
  `[T+0x4c]` verb, copies the box to the stack, appends the class word
  0x98274 at +0x10 - the request block of PR-150/PR-244 - and calls
  0x57500 with the level context from [[0xcef40]+0x390] and the object's
  plane [obj+0x24]; the boxes are then compared the same way. Only when the
  boxes overlap does it go on: `call [T+0x50]`, 0x52d30 (the position
  getter) and `call [T+0x48]` on each side, then 0x42de0 with the results.
  (c) THE PLANE RESCALE 0x57500 is a fixed-point scale: with the plane
  index in edx it computes `imul edx, [ [d+0x20] + 4*plane ]` over
  [d+0x10] and `idiv [ [d+0x1c]*4 + plane ]`, i.e. one multiply/divide
  table per plane; 0x57532 is the same shape with an added
  `add eax, [[d+0x24] + 4*plane]` offset. This is the arithmetic behind the
  parallax planes that `plany=` names.
  (d) THE FAMILY SPLIT. Over the 219 class tables the four geometry verbs
  take exactly two values each, and the split is the family boundary found
  in PR-380: +0x44 = 0x23920 in 186 and 0x23bf0 in 33; +0x48 = 0x23aa0 /
  0x23be0; +0x4c = 0x23a20 / 0x23bd0; +0x50 = 0x53e40 / 0x23bc0. The 33
  tables of the 0x23b50 family answer 0 for the flag word (0x23bf0 is
  `xor eax,eax; ret`), so the 0x1000 and 0x40400 tests at 0x53b1d and
  0x53b3b can never pass for them - that whole family is outside the
  AC_BLOK answer path. Only +0x50 is not a stub in the 186 family: 0x53e40.
GATE: light: verify-index verify-docs rc=0 (ok); nothing under ported/ is
  touched by this record, so the build and level gates were not run; the
  index was regenerated with this record in the tree before the run.
```

- WHY. The F6 thread asks what the lion stands on. This is the step that
  decides whether two objects are considered together at all: same plane,
  compare the authored boxes; different planes, rescale each box by that
  plane's table first. It also says which classes can ever be in that
  conversation - the 33 tables of the second family report no box and no
  flags, so they are excluded by construction.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the same `[T+0x4c]` box verb serves both the
  plain and the rescaled path, with the 0x98274 request block as the only
  difference - the engine treats "a box" and "a box on a named plane" as
  the same object with one extra word.

- WHY. OI-129 asked whether the port's unmodelled `ground_on`
  pair mattered on an ordinary landing. It does not: the measured
  game changes the held-surface answer and keeps the separate
  standing bit clear. The authored vector is present as the live
  pair used by the aim chain, exactly as PR-364's static reading
  said; it is not applied to the player's position in this path.
  The contradiction between the fixture suite and the shipped
  `.SEQ` values is removed without inventing a position snap.

- WHAT SURPRISED ME. That the visible landing was represented by
  an address-valued provider handle rather than the boolean the
  first tracer was built to watch. The object's aim anchors were
  continuously changing with the animation frame, while the flag
  that names PR-354's scripted state stayed untouched.

MEASURED: (a) THE AUTHORED GROUND FILES. The HD ETAPY container (sha
  be5d8b92..., the one the disk-D rig runs; the CD variant holds no `.PLT`
  record at all) carries ten of them, dumped with `tools/re/llrs_cat1
  ETAPY <LEVEL> <NAME>.PLT`: 457 lines, 1749 points. A file's first line
  is a decimal header and it equals the file's line count in 10 of 10.
  Inside every one of the 457 lines x never decreases - the shape 0x45380
  needs. Separator characters that follow the points: ';' 1738, '!' 11,
  '#' 0. ZARIA.01's is named by LEVELDES/ZARIA1.DES: `dir=zaria.01`,
  `platformy=zaria_a.plt`, `blokady=zar.blk`, `sufity=none.des`, next to
  `pozycja=50,640` and `lew=TLewZaria,...`.
  (b) THE CONFIG KEYS AND THEIR LOADERS, ONE FUNCTION. The parser that
  reads a level description compares each entry's key word, held at
  [ebp+0x3a], with the literals at 0x91e1e "platformy", 0x91e2c
  "blokady" and 0x91e38 "sufity" (0x4cf64, 0x4cf94, 0x4cfc7; the compare
  is 0x76d20, a word-at-a-time string equality) and stores the value with
  the format " %s" (0x91e28) through 0x57d30 into [ebp+0x7a],
  [ebp+0x8a], [ebp+0x9a]. An entry that matches no key ends at 0x4d423
  with the error string "Bledny wpis w pliku levels: %s" (0x91ee5) - the
  engine calls this file a levels file. The SAME function then opens each
  name with 0x4a910 ([ebp+0x8a] at 0x4d440, [ebp+0x7a] at 0x4d466,
  [ebp+0x9a] at 0x4d48c; 0x4a910 resolves the name and leaves the stream
  at the globals 0x961fc/0x96200 that the line reader 0x49820 reads) and
  hands the stream to the matching loader: 0x4db50 at 0x4d44f, 0x4dc00 at
  0x4d472, 0x4da90 at 0x4d49b. So `platformy=` is the ground table,
  `blokady=` is the 0x4db50 table, `sufity=` the 0x4da90 one - the
  mapping ZARIA1.DES's three lines suggested is now machine-code fact.
  0x4dc30 scans the header with "%d" (0x91f27) into [world+0x80];
  0x4dc55 asks 0x76a64 for count*12+4 bytes; 0x4dc7f stores the array at
  [world+0x74]; 0x4dc88 walks it 12 bytes a step and 0x4dc92 calls
  `[element class + 0x20]` with edx = the running text pointer: one line
  per element. The siblings read their headers with the same "%d"
  (0x91f21, 0x91f24) into [world+0x84] and [world+0x7c], and 0x4db50
  keeps 20-byte elements at [world+0x70] and parses each by calling
  0x455e0 directly.
  (c) THE ELEMENT AND ITS POINT RECORDS, 0x45120. "%d" at [element+8] is
  the line's vertex count, i.e. points-1. 0x45149 allocates
  (count+1)*13+4 bytes in 13-byte records with element class base
  0xa0c64, stored at [element+4]. 0x4a0b0 reads `%d,%d` (0x91d0f) into
  record+0x0 and record+0x4. Between the pairs 0x45130 scans " %c"
  (0x91830) and 0x4519d writes 1 for ';', 2 for '#' and 0 for anything
  else into that record's +0xc; 0x451e2 then consumes the terminating ';'
  through 0x498f0 with the literal ';' at 0x91834. A point record is
  therefore {int x, int y, dword class word, byte flag}.
  (d) THE CLASS WORDS ARE PR-372's CONTAINER. The method array at 0xa0cb4
  read at base +0xc, i.e. 0xa0cc0, has 0x45120 at +0x20 - the verb
  0x4dc92 calls - and 0x45250 at +0x8, which is exactly the table PR-372
